subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = π, prove that cos²A + cos²B − cos²C = 1 − 2 sin A sin B cos C.

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.99, chapter 8 TRANSFORMATIONS, Long Answer question 2(i). The book prints TRANSFORMATIONS as a separate un-numbered chapter-style banner immediately after chapter 8's VSAQ run and restarts its numbering at 1; we ship both under one unit, ordered by the syllabus, and never mirror the book's arrangement. NUMBERING RECORDED, NOT RENUMBERED: the "2." and "i)" labels sit in the binding gutter of the scan and are unreadable, so the printed stem reads as unnumbered; the number above is the position in the run, not a label we can read on the page. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+3+2+1+1 split rewards the two substantial transformations — the sum-to-product pairing and the use of the angle condition — over the set-up and the finish, and it is the same split and the same step ids already carried by the sibling cards of this family (sin2a_sum, cos2a_sum, sin_half_squares, cos_half_squares), deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities, so a student who learns the arc once can attempt any of them. IDENTITY CHECKED NUMERICALLY before and after writing, and every intermediate line of the derivation with it: at A = 50°, B = 60°, C = 70° both sides equal 0.5461981327, and the identity holds again at (40°, 75°, 65°) and (110°, 25°, 45°). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C carries the long answers at 8 marks each under the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27), any 2 of 3; the Transformations slot is always a question of this kind. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. These are squared terms, so no sum-to-product formula applies yet. The condition is still written first, because it is used twice further down.
steps.memory_tip: A + B = π − C. Written first, it is used twice: once on cos(A+B) and once inside the bracket.
lines: A + B + C = π  ⇒  A + B = π − C

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first as A plus B equals pi minus C
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is false, so this line is the hypothesis the whole proof depends on, not preamble.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Squared terms carry no sum-to-product formula, so one of them is turned into 1 − sin². That single move produces the leading 1 and sets up a difference of squares.
steps.memory_tip: Turn cos²B into 1 − sin²B. That gives the leading 1 and leaves cos²A − sin²B, which has its own formula.

recall.must_convey: That one squared cosine is written as 1 − sin², so that a 1 appears and cos²A − sin²B is left.
accept: write cos squared B as one minus sin squared B so the one appears and a difference of squares is left
convert one term to get one plus cos squared A minus sin squared B
replace the second cosine squared with one minus sine squared
cos square B ni one minus sin square B ga rasi, difference of squares techukovali
turn one of them into one minus sin squared

steps.why: cos²A − sin²B = cos(A+B) cos(A−B) is the formula that replaces sum-to-product for squared terms, and it needs one cosine square minus one sine square.
common_mistakes: Converting all three terms and losing track.
Turning cos²A into 1 − sin²A as well, which destroys the difference of squares.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The difference of squares becomes a product, and the condition then turns cos(A+B) into −cos C so that every term after the 1 carries cos C.
steps.memory_tip: cos(π − C) = −cos C, with the MINUS. That sign is what collects both terms under cos C.

recall.must_convey: That cos²A − sin²B = cos(A+B) cos(A−B) is applied, and cos(A+B) then becomes −cos C.
accept: use cos squared minus sin squared equals cos of the sum times cos of the difference, then cos of pi minus C is minus cos C
apply the difference of squares identity and substitute the angle condition
the cosine of A plus B becomes minus cos C
cos pi minus C ante minus cos C
convert using the angle condition so every term has cos C
heard_as: cos A plus B cos A minus B

steps.why: The condition converts an expression in A and B into one in C. Only after that do the remaining two terms share a factor.
common_mistakes: Using the formula on cos²A − cos²B, where it does not apply.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The 1 is set aside and cos C comes out; the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that the bracket becomes a difference of two cosines.
steps.memory_tip: There is no 2 to take out here — only cos C. Then cos C = −cos(A+B) makes the bracket a difference.

recall.must_convey: That cos C alone is taken out as the common factor and rewritten inside the bracket as −cos(A+B).
accept: keep the one outside and take cos C common, then cos C becomes minus cos A plus B
factor out cos C so the bracket is a difference of cosines
the bracket becomes cos A minus B minus cos A plus B
cos C common teesi, cos C ni minus cos A plus B ga marchali
use the condition a second time so the bracket subtracts

steps.why: The right-hand side carries sin A sin B, and only a difference of cosines gives a product of sines.
common_mistakes: Taking out 2 cos C when there is no 2.
Leaving the bracket as a sum, which would give cosines instead of sines.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One product formula finishes it. The coefficient on the answer is 2, not 4, because only cos C was taken out and not 2 cos C.
steps.memory_tip: The answer carries 2, not 4 — the factor taken out was cos C alone.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A−B) − cos(A+B) = 2 sinA sinB is applied, giving 1 − 2 sinA sinB cosC.
accept: use cos A minus B minus cos A plus B equals two sin A sin B to get one minus two sin A sin B cos C
the bracket becomes two sin A sin B so the answer is one minus two sin A sin B cos C
apply the product formula and keep the one
cos difference formula tho two sin A sin B vasthundi, one minus two sin A sin B cos C
the final answer is one minus two sin A sin B cos C

steps.why: cos(A−B) − cos(A+B) = 2 sin A sin B gives the two sine factors, and the 2 it brings is the whole coefficient of the answer.
common_mistakes: Writing 4 sin A sin B cos C by carrying a 2 that was never taken out.
Losing the leading 1 at the very end.
